title: Why do virtual threads change the concurrency model but NOT the system capacity — DB pool, CPU, downstream limits remain — and why is backpressure and measuring bottlenecks essential?
shortTitle: Do virtual threads change system capacity?

s1_definition.profdef: Virtual threads remove the THREAD bottleneck (millions cheap) but leave every OTHER constraint untouched: DB connection pool (still 100), CPU cores (still 8), downstream API rate limit (still 500 RPS), memory, locks. 20,000 VTs all awaiting a 100-connection DB pool = 19,900 queued. Firing 500K VTs at a 500-RPS downstream = self-inflicted DDoS. You MUST keep: backpressure (reject excess work), bounded concurrency (Semaphore), timeouts (CompletableFuture.orTimeout), and circuit breakers. Rule: measure the REAL bottleneck before migrating — if the DB was the limit, VTs won't help.
s1_definition.analogy: Opening unlimited bank token counters (VTs) doesn't increase the number of tellers (DB connections) or the vault's cash (CPU). 100,000 tokens waiting for 10 tellers = massive queue. The bank needs bouncers (backpressure), queue limits (Semaphore), and time limits (timeouts) even with unlimited tokens.
s1_definition.oneliner: VTs remove thread bottleneck, NOT resource bottleneck. DB pool, CPU, rate limits unchanged. Keep backpressure + Semaphore + timeouts. Measure real bottleneck FIRST.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Virtual threads remove the THREAD bottleneck (millions cheap) but leave every OTHER constraint untouched: DB connection pool (still 100), CPU cores (still 8), downstream API rate limit (still 500 RPS), memory, locks. 20,000 VTs all awaiting a 100-connection DB pool = 19,900 queued. Firing 500K VTs at a 500-RPS downstream = self-inflicted DDoS. You MUST keep: backpressure (reject excess work), bounded concurrency (Semaphore), timeouts (CompletableFuture.orTimeout), and circuit breakers. Rule: measure the REAL bottleneck before migrating — if the DB was the limit, VTs won't help.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Opening unlimited bank token counters (VTs) doesn't increase the number of tellers (DB connections) or the vault's cash (CPU). 100,000 tokens waiting for 10 tellers = massive queue. The bank needs bouncers (backpressure), queue limits (Semaphore), and time limits (timeouts) even with unlimited tokens.

**One line to remember:** VTs remove thread bottleneck, NOT resource bottleneck. DB pool, CPU, rate limits unchanged. Keep backpressure + Semaphore + timeouts. Measure real bottleneck FIRST.

sections.s2_technical:
Virtual threads increase how many tasks can be IN FLIGHT concurrently, but they do not increase the system's actual CAPACITY. The real limits remain: the database connection pool size, the number of CPU cores for compute, downstream service rate limits, and memory. If the database accepts 100 connections, spawning a million virtual threads that all want a connection just means 999,900 of them wait.

The correct mental model: virtual threads remove the THREAD as a bottleneck so you can express high concurrency simply, but you must still bound access to every finite downstream resource (connection pools, rate limiters, bulkheads). Otherwise you convert "thread exhaustion" into "connection-pool exhaustion" or "downstream overload" — the queue just moves.

A banking example: a service can accept 50,000 concurrent requests on virtual threads, but the ledger database still allows 100 connections, so a `Semaphore(100)` or a sized connection pool must gate DB access; the fraud API still allows 500 requests/second, so a rate limiter must gate that. Senior nuance: adopting virtual threads is not a capacity upgrade — size your connection pools, rate limiters, and CPU-bound executors deliberately, and treat virtual threads as a concurrency-expression tool, not a scaling silver bullet.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A team switched to virtual threads expecting more throughput, but the ledger database still allowed only 100 connections, so overload simply moved from thread exhaustion to connection-pool exhaustion. Fix: keep the connection pool and a rate limiter sized to the real downstream limits; virtual threads express concurrency but do not raise actual capacity.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: a service with 50,000 virtual threads, a DB pool of 100, 8 CPU cores, and a 500/sec rate limit.

**Step 2.** Virtual threads let all 50,000 requests be expressed concurrently at almost no thread cost.

**Step 3.** But each request still needs a DB connection (max 100), a CPU slice (8 cores), and a rate-limited API call (500/sec).

**Step 4.** The effective capacity is the MINIMUM of those real limits — here 8 for CPU-bound work — not 50,000.

**Step 5.** Spawning more virtual threads beyond the bottleneck only makes them wait; capacity is unchanged.

```text
INFO: virtualThreads=50000 but effectiveCapacity=min(100,8,500)=8
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ BOTTLENECK ANALYSIS ═══

  Resource              Before VTs         After VTs          Changed?
  ────────────────────  ─────────────────  ─────────────────  ────────
  Threads               200 (bottleneck!)  200,000 (no limit) YES (Recommended) 
  DB connections         100               100                NO (Avoid) 
  CPU cores              8                 8                  NO (Avoid) 
  Downstream API RPS     500               500                NO (Avoid) 
  Memory                 16 GB             16 GB              NO (Avoid) 

  If threads WERE the bottleneck → VTs help! (Recommended) 
  If DB pool WAS the bottleneck → VTs DON'T help! (Avoid) 
  Rule: MEASURE the real bottleneck BEFORE migrating to VTs.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Virtual threads change the concurrency model (millions of cheap threads) but NOT the system's capacity. Every constraint besides thread count remains: DB pool size, CPU cores, downstream rate limits, memory, and lock contention. Migrating to VTs when the DB was the bottleneck is a no-op — you get the same throughput with more memory consumption. Always measure the real bottleneck first. If the bottleneck was thread count (common in I/O-heavy web servers), VTs help dramatically. If it was DB connections, add connection pooling and Semaphore gating. Keep backpressure (reject excess), timeouts (don't wait forever), and circuit breakers regardless.
